question: A mother brings her 8-month-old for a well-child visit. The child has been receiving only thin rice gruel once a day since 6 months. What is the most appropriate complementary feeding advice per WHO IYCF guidelines?

answers.text: Continue thin rice gruel but increase to three times per day

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thin gruel provides inadequate energy density and only one food group. At 8 months, the child needs thicker, varied foods (mashed/pureed consistency) from multiple food groups 2–3 times per day, not just increased frequency of the same thin preparation.

answers.text: Introduce thick mashed foods from multiple food groups 2–3 times daily, continuing breastfeeding on demand

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. At 6–8 months, WHO recommends: thickly mashed/pureed consistency (not thin gruel), 2–3 meals/day, foods from multiple food groups (cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruits, and if acceptable — egg/meat/fish), with continued breastfeeding. Thin gruel alone is inadequate for energy needs.

answers.text: Introduce family foods (chapati, rice) since the child is already 8 months old

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Family foods are appropriate only from 12 months. At 8 months, foods should be specially prepared — mashed or pureed to a consistency the infant can safely swallow. Introducing hard or lumpy family foods too early risks choking and poor intake.

answers.text: Discontinue breastfeeding and switch to formula so complementary food intake improves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Breastfeeding should continue to at least 2 years alongside complementary foods. Formula is not recommended as a breastfeeding replacement in this context. The issue is inadequate complementary feeding quality, not the breastfeeding itself.

overallFeedback.feedback: At 6–8 months: thickly mashed foods from 2+ food groups, 2–3 times daily, with continued breastfeeding. Thin gruel is inadequate in energy density and micronutrients.
Well done! The key problems here are thin consistency, insufficient frequency, and lack of dietary diversity — all correctable with proper counselling.
